entry.title: New Records Clarify Housing Counts and Funding Decisions
entry.content:
New Records Clarify Housing Counts and Funding Decisions

Published: November 7, 2026, 9:30 a.m. MST (Tucson).

What’s Included in the Housing Count?

The City’s draft describes 378 units as newly constructed, but 96 at Casa del Pueblo are existing apartments being rehabilitated. Other projects in the list remain under construction. The figure is not a verified count of completed new homes. City permit

Which Grant Was Reduced?

The submitted priority list identifies SAAF’s AVP rapid-rehousing grant as the roughly 50% reduction: $792,695 was involuntarily reallocated for underspending, followed by reallocation of the balance because of limited renewal space. The separate payment-system-lockout case remains unidentified. Final HUD awards are unverified. Priority list

Where Does Craycroft Stand?

The City’s posted resolution states that Council adopted authorization for up to $10 million in bonds. Federal records show an environmental milestone and a submitted financing plan for the 82-unit preservation project. Closing, proceeds and signed assistance contracts remain unverified. City resolution · RAD data

What About El Portal?

The City reports that 41 households moved into existing El Portal apartments over the summer with Housing First assistance. That is separate from the planned voucher expansion, whose final HUD approval and signed contracts remain unverified. City report

What Happened to the CDBG Transfer?

The official action report confirms Council adopted the $1.5 million transfer between funding categories on October 6. It did not increase total funding. HUD submission, implementation and spending remain open questions. Council action report

Housing Funding and Project Questions

Posted: November 6, 2026, 7:42 a.m. MST (Tucson). Source dates are identified below.

Follow documented allocations toward spending and completed work, approved assistance toward signed contracts and residents served, and project plans toward verified budgets and homes.

  • Funding: federal allocations, Craycroft financing and the CoC request.
  • Projects and outcomes: Craycroft, El Portal and Housing First.
  • Open questions: project costs, named and unnamed CoC funding decisions, and CDBG.

Funding requests and proposed actions are not final awards, closed financing or verified resident placements. The named Housing First partial reallocation is separate from the unnamed 50% case. Review the dated sources.

entry.title: Housing Plans: Confirmed Actions and Open Questions
entry.content:
Housing Plans: Confirmed Actions and Open Questions

Review snapshot: November 5, 2026, 8:39 a.m. MST (Tucson, UTC−7). Original source dates differ.

El Portal Voucher Expansion

The August 18 PHA Legal Action Report records an 8–0 vote adopting PHA2026-56 as amended, approving plan changes to allow noncompetitive PBV allocation for units owned by the PHA and its nonprofit subsidiary, EPHD. Legal Action Report

The October 30 HCD memo reports that the August 18 PHA plan approval permits up to 120 El Portal PBV units in the 2026 plan year, with 181 planned across two phases and approximately $1.15 million in additional annual rent revenue, subject to rent reasonableness. Implementation depends on vouchers, approvals, inspections, and eligibility reviews. These are plans, not confirmed placements or vacancies. Memo, pages 2–3

The policy package also describes 70 or more additional units in 2027. Phase sizes need clarification: 120 is a cap, not a confirmed first-phase count. Its December 1 effective date appears in a document still marked REVIEW AND APPROVAL DRAFT; adoption is not established. Policy package, PDF pages 3 and 5

Craycroft Figures Need Reconciliation

The November 5 presentation lists 82 units on two slides, but 124 versus 85 bedrooms. An August environmental review estimates $33,894,857, consistent with the pipeline table’s rounded “$33.9” entry. The detailed November slide gives $34.7 million. These may reflect different estimates or scopes; their relationship needs clarification. Environmental review, page 4 · Presentation, pages 12 and 31

The pipeline’s displayed costs sum to 590.8, versus its printed 593.5. If all entries mean millions, that is a $2.7 million arithmetic difference. The table needs clarification; this is not evidence of missing money or overruns.

Bond Capacity Documented

Arizona Finance Authority’s October 7 tracker records a $10 million volume-cap allocation, approved February 9, expiring December 15. Issue-price and closing-date fields are blank in that snapshot. This is financing capacity, not a grant, proof of issuance, or confirmation of the November 4 City vote. Tracker, project BX260130022

Community Preference Remains in Development

The City says no Community Preference Policy or predetermined design exists yet. Recommendations are targeted for May–June 2027, not a current preference for applicants. Presentation, pages 3 and 10

CEHD meets November 5, 4–6 p.m. Tucson time. This briefing precedes that meeting and does not imply approval of its proposals. Agenda

Follow-up added November 7, 2026, 9:30 a.m. MST (Tucson): November 7 records clarify the housing count, grant reduction, financing, El Portal placements and CDBG adoption. The earlier review above is retained as history.

entry.title: Pima County’s Housing Report: Counts and Averages Need Clarification
entry.content:
Pima County’s Housing Report: Counts and Averages Need Clarification

Published: November 6, 2026, 4:48 p.m. MST (Tucson). Source: November 5, 2026 County memo, pages 2–3.

What Did the County Report?

Pima County reported $2.49 million spent and 925 households served across six housing assistance strategies in the first quarter of FY27. The figures are subject to reconciliation; the report does not say whether households appear in more than one category.

What Doesn’t Add Up?

  • Rapid rehousing: The table lists 95 households, but the narrative totals 98.
  • Rapid-rehousing average: The reported costs divided by 95 equal $3,671.42, not the printed $3,290.42.
  • Home-repair average: The reported costs divided by 91 equal $2,279.52, not the printed $2,280.52.

What Funding Is Involved?

The $207,436 home-repair line is listed under County CDBG agencies. CDBG is a federal HUD program, but the memo doesn’t identify the specific award. It separately lists $111,045 as the County-funded portion of Affordable Housing Fund repair and weatherization work.

What’s Next?

A reconciled table and an explanation of the counts and calculations would clarify the results. The discrepancies alone do not establish misuse of funds.

Source: Pima County, One Pima Initiative: Fiscal Year 27 First Quarter Update, November 5, 2026, page 2; rapid-rehousing narrative, page 3.

Corrected source mappings for the CDBG approval recap and Craycroft/Lee Street finding, clarified the findings summary and completed reconciliation milestone, and attributed El Portal’s 120-unit limit to the October 30 memo. Figures and original source dates are unchanged.

  • SRC-060: October 9 City approval recap now supports F-001 and Q-006. SRC-071 remains the separate proposal notice.
  • F-003’s public data points to SRC-064 for Craycroft/Lee Street; unrelated Amazon Flats source SRC-065 remains available for the findings and questions it supports.
  • The 12 finding entries include 9 dated observations, 2 open comparisons and 1 resolved comparison (F-006). The published CDBG reconciliation remains linked; its regular-CDBG narrative difference is still open.

These are reference and presentation corrections, not new funding or housing-outcome findings. Existing source IDs, resident-privacy safeguards and earlier correction history are retained. The evidence index now has 14 source entries.

entry.title: Questions Corrected to Protect Residents’ Privacy
entry.content:
Questions Corrected to Protect Residents’ Privacy

We revised our questions to request aggregate counts and appropriately redacted records, without identifying residents. We also clarified other questions to avoid unsupported conclusions. The figures, sources and findings remain unchanged.

Summary revised: November 6, 2026, 9:52 a.m. MST (Tucson). Original correction history and source dates follow unchanged.

Corrected: November 6, 2026, 8:09 a.m. MST (Tucson).

Earlier El Portal wording asked about the identities of residents receiving assistance and the specific units under contract. The corrected question asks how many units are covered by signed contracts and how many households are receiving assistance, as of the reporting date. Q-016 and its linked summaries now seek aggregate counts, not resident identities or individual case records.

We reviewed all 20 numbered questions and related prompts across the site. Q-008 now seeks project-level, nonduplicative totals instead of occupied-unit identifiers. Q-009, Q-012 and Q-015 specify aggregate counts and public or appropriately redacted records. Q-017 asks for broad destination categories, inclusion rules and denominators, with small groups combined or suppressed where people could be identified. Related report and findings requests were clarified the same way.

Q-001, Q-005, Q-018 and Q-020 were also reworded to ask neutral, specific questions without implying an unsupported conclusion. Project and agency identities remain part of public accountability. Stable question IDs, documented figures, source dates, reporting periods and uncertainty limits are unchanged. This is a wording correction, not new evidence or a new finding about any agency or resident. See the resident privacy standard.

entry.title: Tucson’s CDBG Funding: What Adds Up, and What Still Needs Explaining
entry.content:
Tucson’s CDBG Funding: What Adds Up, and What Still Needs Explaining

We withdrew the earlier $944,972.60 comparison because it combined regular CDBG and CDBG-CV, which are reported separately. The $1,284,589.71 difference within regular CDBG remains unexplained; it does not establish missing funds.

Summary revised: November 6, 2026, 9:52 a.m. MST (Tucson). Original correction history and source dates follow unchanged.

Posted: November 6, 2026, 7:42 a.m. MST (Tucson). Source dates are identified below.

What Did We Find, and Why Does It Matter?

The resource figures and ending balance in Tucson’s CDBG reports add up. The remaining question is more focused: how does the City’s spending narrative connect to the corrected financial report for its regular CDBG program? Federal guidance now helps separate that question from coronavirus-response funding. Financial summary · Spending narrative · OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61

For residents, the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) can mean home repairs, better public facilities and services for low-income people. Connecting the dollars to completed work helps show what that funding delivered. City’s description of CDBG-supported work

What Adds Up?

Program income, money generated by CDBG-funded activities, accounts for the previously questioned resource difference. The full financial report also includes money carried over from the previous year:

  • $5,068,664 annual grant + $349,468 program income = $5,418,132. The income is already included; adding it again would double-count it.
  • $3,778,221.56 opening balance + $5,418,132 grant and income = $9,196,353.56 in total resources.
  • $9,196,353.56 resources − $4,717,936.37 expenditures = $4,478,417.19 ending balance.

Those calculations reproduce the City’s resource total and ending balance. The reported balance does not establish money available for new work today. Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

Which Spending Figures Should We Compare?

The Office of Management and Budget’s 2025 Compliance Supplement says the standard PR26 CDBG Financial Summary Report has been restricted to annual formula grants since September 14, 2020. A separate PR26 report covers CDBG-CV, the CARES Act coronavirus-response grants. OMB reporting guidance, PDF p. 61

That makes the regular CDBG figures the appropriate starting point:

  • Corrected standard PR-26 expenditures: $4,717,936.37.
  • CDBG spending stated in the narrative: $3,433,346.66.
  • Difference requiring reconciliation: $1,284,589.71.

The summary table’s $4,717,936 agrees with the corrected PR-26 after rounding. The narrative says the final CDBG draw occurred after June 30, 2025, which may help explain the difference. But the records reviewed do not show which transactions connect the two figures or establish that timing explains the full amount. Summary table and narrative, PDF p. 13 · Corrected PR-26, PDF p. 149

Why Set Aside the Earlier $944,972.60 Comparison?

That calculation subtracted both the $3,433,346.66 CDBG narrative and the $339,616.74 CDBG-CV narrative from the rounded $4,717,936 summary total. It mixed the separately reported grant programs. In light of the federal reporting guidance, it should not be presented as a second comparable spending gap. The question to pursue is the $1,284,589.71 difference within the regular CDBG figures. City narrative · OMB reporting guidance

Does the City’s Separate Correction Resolve This?

The City says $102,106.09 in public-service costs was assigned to PY2024 instead of PY2023, and that its HUD field representative approved the correction. We reviewed that City statement, not a separate HUD approval record.

The adjustment appears on line 30 of the PR-26, in the public-service-limit calculation. Line 14, the adjustment to total expenditures, is zero. Subtracting the public-service adjustment from total spending would treat a cap adjustment as an adjustment to total expenditures. This correction does not, by itself, explain the narrative difference. Correction explanation and PR-26, PDF pp. 148–149

What Would Make the Picture Clearer?

The corrected PR-26 is available and includes activity and voucher detail. The next step is to connect those records to:

  • A line-by-line explanation bridging the $3,433,346.66 CDBG narrative to the $4,717,936.37 corrected total, identifying transactions recorded after year-end and keeping CDBG-CV separate.
  • Commitments, restrictions and later transactions affecting the reported balance.
  • Completed work and aggregate beneficiary counts from the same reporting period. PR-26 activity detail, PDF p. 150

How Far Do These Findings Go?

The $1,284,589.71 is an arithmetic difference between reported amounts that still needs a transaction-level explanation. This review does not establish missing funds, currently available assistance or a cost per housing outcome.

This is independent public-record research, not a governmental or certified financial audit. Reporting period: July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025. Corrected PR-26 dated March 13, 2026. City CAPER and OMB guidance rechecked November 6, 2026, Tucson time.
